item.title: 1Password Security Incident
item.description:
Source: 1password.com

Top Comment:

This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.

In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.

Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.

I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

item.description:
Source: github.com

See also Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: the magnitude of what’s now happening - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50646108

Top Comment:

For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked, https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/).

They include: #25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture.

#89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for #64 — Mean-payoff games, #65 — Parity games, #340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games.

#183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes, #130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart.

#137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound.

(rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).

Think of your supporters:

Think of all of the people who have helped you get to where you are today. All of the coaches, advisers, supporters, teachers, employers, mentors, relatives and friends.

All the people who helped you in the early days of your career, or in your life, or recently. All of the references who spoke on your behalf for jobs. Select one or two, and write them a handwritten note to let them know how you are doing and to thank them for helping you get here.

We are all on both sides of this equation from time to time, and we all know how much we enjoy hearing from those whose lives we have influenced, especially hearing those simple and magical words, “Thank you.” To me, it feels like more than ever, we need to find moments of gratitude.

I hope your doing this adds a little extra meaning to your Thanksgiving and to the Thanksgiving of those who will be hearing from you! Based on the moving experiences many of you have shared with me that resulted from this simple gesture, I am confident that you will find this rewarding.

For those of you who will be celebrating American Thanksgiving, I hope you enjoy what I know is a much-needed break. And for those of you who are not, I hope you will join me in a few moments of gratitude.

I’ve had OpenAI and Anthropic accounts continuously for a long time, with a sampling of others rotating in and out.

The back-and-forth between which provider is more generous has been interesting to follow because the balance has been swinging back and forth. Not long ago I was having fun throwing OpenAI tokens at a side project because they felt limitless between the allowances and the constant flow of resets. Then Opus 5.5 came along and gave even more usage without any reset shenanigans to try to stay ahead of. OpenAI responded by reducing their allowances, and now the reset party seems to have stopped as well.

Now they’re sending us vague emails about limits being adjusted downward again, citing a billing error? The original email was so vague that they had to send a clarification because it didn’t have enough information to tell if we were going to be retroactively penalized or if it only applied going forward.

This comes at the same time as they’re rolling out a change that makes chat quota subtract from your coding quota, which removes one of the last remaining big selling points of an OpenAI subscription in a world where Opus 5.5 exists.

I would love to have some insights into what’s happening at OpenAI right now. From the outside it feels like something substantial changed in how they approach everything, but the weird part is how it’s coming at the worst possible time for them to be appearing like the lesser deal. Did they finally get the internal marching orders to turn the profitability knob up and ignore everything else?

item.title: Smart people who give a shit use tools
item.description:
Source: www.iankduncan.com

Top Comment:

Something really bothers me about the "it's just another higher-level abstraction" argument but I can't quite nail down what.

Using an LLM is a completely different experience from moving to assembler to C, or C to Javascript. The nature of the activity you are performing in those transitions in the same, moving to an LLM is not. Even if you are writing in Javascript, you are still modelling a problem on to some representation in code. The only thing that is abstracted from you is memory management, a technical detail.

With an LLM you don't model the problem at all, you let something else do it. Moving from an low-code app builder to an LLM is a higher level of abstraction. Moving from writing code yourself to having an LLM write it is something different entirely.

(Though the author seems to be advocating against that style of usage, which I agree with.)

item.title: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp
item.description:
Source: devnull.land

Top Comment:

Early in 2025 a bunch of folks realized that AMD made a bunch of cards with mediocre compute but incredibly fast HBM2 memory in their circa 2018 gfx906 datacenter series, so you could get 32GB VRAM capable of incredible 1 TB / s bandwidth for $200 (the closest in today’s cards is north of $3000)

There has been a rich little ecosystem of folks optimizing llama.cpp for these odd cards (no tensor cores, no native bf16 etc.) including my little personal repo https://github.com/kinchahoy/llama-of-vega.cpp. Stuff like this focused on more modern RDNA doesn’t help us at all.

It’s been interesting to see how much each new frontier model can figure out in terms of optimizing for these GPUs and what they can’t!

Fable and Astra will regularly run out of ideas until I point them to someone’s actually thoughtful repo and then they’ll diligently incorporate ideas.

The optimization wins are huge (I was initially skeptical that per model kernel optimizations would be worth much). 27B at a pristine Q8 quant goes from base llama.cpp at some 250 pp / 25 tg to 600 pp / 40 tg even before speculative decoding.

item.title: The short age of dragon riders
item.description:
Source: atilloy.com

Top Comment:

It's a well written article, but I disagree with it completely. It doesn't seem entirely internally cohesive. First, he says this:

> As of November 2026, the best public models still lack research taste. They execute beautifully when given a clear goal but are worse than the best researchers at coming up with good questions, or at having the sparks of creativity needed to get out of a dead end. They do not have as much vision as the best humans.

I agree! But then, apparently through the magic of RLVR, he somehow thinks that models will someday suddenly accrue this taste.

Why hasn't that happened yet? I get just as frustrated when I let Fable 5.2 make product decisions as I did with ChatGPT4. They solve the problems I give them much better, but when I try to let them lead to the next milestone, they consistently choose the worst, most conservative option.

> To do great things, we need to forgo some understanding of what is going on at lower levels, to focus on higher ones

If we don't understand the lower levels, how will we ensure that the "research taste" is good? How will we have any idea whether we are pushing towards the right kind of discoveries? It doesn't make any sense!

You can pretend that this is the same as something like my day job as a web developer. I don't fully understand how the hardware works at an atomic level. However, I have found that every time I learn more about the foundations on which my abstractions are built, I make better decisions in my job even though that knowledge is technically unnecessary. Understanding pointers in C finally made me understand object references in JavaScript, and it helped me to write more efficient code.

We need to understand what's happening underneath to some degree if we're going to build on top of it prudently.
